title: Connectivity and Fiber Faults
summary: Reason about physical connectivity and fiber fault clues using safe simulated links.
objectives: Compare synthetic symptoms for cable, switch, transceiver, and path problems.
Explain the safety boundary between classroom models and professional fiber work.

vocab.def: A device that sends and receives signals.
A condition that prevents a system from working as expected.

sections.heading: Physical links matter
sections.body: A server can have power and still be unreachable if a cable, port, transceiver, switch path, or fiber link has a fault. Synthetic diagrams can show where evidence points.

sections.heading: Fiber carries information with light
sections.body: Fiber supports high-capacity connections over distance. In class, use paper, yarn, diagrams, or a simulator to model paths.

sections.heading: Professional work requires training
sections.body: Do not inspect live fiber, handle glass fragments, use lasers, or operate termination tools without qualified training. Classroom activities stay unpowered and simulated.

practice.prompt: Compare two synthetic diagrams: one with a disconnected link and one with a failed switch port. List evidence that distinguishes them.

quiz.question: What is a safe Grade 10 fiber activity?
options: Tracing a simulated fiber path with a diagram or model
Inspecting a live fiber with your eyes
quiz.answer: Tracing a simulated fiber path with a diagram or model

lab.objective: Trace safe classroom cable and simulated fiber paths, then document a synthetic fault.

reflectionPrompt: Why is knowing when not to inspect a live fiber system part of technical professionalism?
